title: A Bridge for the Typewriter
premise: In 1937, on a storm-battered island off the coast, Coral Okafor keeps the lighthouse alone after her husband's death, measuring her life in what can be packed into one trunk. When census taker Elias Brandt arrives and asks about the letters she hides—correspondence with Heinrich, the German lighthouse engineer who taught her husband his trade before the war—Coral's careful invisibility begins to crack. As the great storms of that winter isolate the island, Coral must choose between destroying the letters that could brand her a traitor or honoring Heinrich's desperate plea to shelter his daughter, who is fleeing across the water. The novel ends with Coral guiding the girl through the final storm, testifying before a tribunal, and discovering that the family she thought she'd lost has been assembling around her all along.
about_author: Kestrel Winterbourne is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing lighthouse keepers' logs along the northern coasts. Their fiction draws on the marginalia, unsent letters, and weather-stained pages they were never supposed to read too closely.

chapters.title: What Fits in One Trunk
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Establishes her ritual of packing and unpacking the same trunk, her late husband Tomás's typewriter gathering salt-spray rust, and the orders that could come any day transferring her from the light. Emotional beat: grief disguised as practicality.

chapters.title: The Man with the Census Book
chapters.summary: Elias Brandt arrives by supply boat to count the island's souls. Coral answers carefully until he asks where she learned German. She lies; he notices. His POV reveals he's cataloguing 'persons of interest,' not just counting them. Beat: first intrusion.

chapters.title: Letters Under the Lens Plate
chapters.summary: Coral retrieves Heinrich's last letter hidden inside the lens housing: his daughter Greta will come by fishing boat when the storms break, and Coral must keep her. Flashback to 1920s peacetime, when Heinrich and Tomás worked the light together. Beat: the promise made real again.

chapters.title: Inventory of a Marriage
chapters.summary: Coral sorts Tomás's effects for the requisition officer, finding his half-typed memoir naming Heinrich as 'brother.' She must decide what survives the censor. Elias returns, ostensibly to verify figures. Beat: memory as both burden and evidence.

chapters.title: The Storm Season Opens
chapters.summary: First great gale; the light fails briefly and Coral nearly dies relighting it. The islanders—fisherman Dara, shopkeeper Mrs. Quill—begin quietly leaving food at her door. Beat: found family stirring without being named.

chapters.title: A Question Too Many
chapters.summary: Elias confronts Coral directly: he knows about the letters, offers to lose his notes if she tells him the truth. She refuses, but gives him tea and Tomás's chair. His POV: doubt creeping into duty. Beat: enemy becomes ambiguous.

chapters.title: Greta at the Window
chapters.summary: A fishing boat makes landfall in fog; a soaked young woman speaks broken English and Heinrich's name. Coral hides her in the lamp room as the patrol boat sweeps past. Beat: terror and fierce, sudden tenderness.

chapters.title: Three Plates, Three Cups
chapters.summary: Domestic chapter: teaching Greta the light's rhythms, Greta repairing the typewriter with an engineer's hands. Coral catches herself setting three cups out. Beat: belonging arriving uninvited and welcome.

chapters.title: Mrs. Quill Knows
chapters.summary: Mrs. Quill deduces the truth from flour quantities and says nothing—but leaves a second coat, boots, ration cards. The island's silent conspiracy forms. Beat: community as quiet resistance.

chapters.title: Elias Reads the File
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Back on the mainland, he files his report omitting the German connection, then discovers his superior already suspects him. He requests reassignment back to the island. Beat: the watcher becomes watched.

chapters.title: The Trunk Packed Twice
chapters.summary: Orders finally arrive: the light is to be automated and Coral transferred. She packs the trunk—and then unpacks it, realizing leaving means abandoning Greta mid-crossing plan. Beat: the central choice crystallizes.

chapters.title: Dara's Boat
chapters.summary: Fisherman Dara agrees to run Greta to a neutral port, but the storm window is narrowing and patrols have doubled. Coral trades her husband's chronometer for fuel. Beat: sacrifice measured in objects.

chapters.title: Interrogation by Lamplight
chapters.summary: A security officer arrives unannounced; Coral endures questioning while Greta hides beneath the floorboards, listening to Coral lie with steady hands. Beat: courage as performance, terror underneath.

chapters.title: The Typewriter Speaks
chapters.summary: Greta types the finished translation of Tomás's memoir—their joint testimony of friendship across nations—as insurance and inheritance. Coral reads her husband's voice for the first time since his death. Beat: grief transmuted into legacy.

chapters.title: Elias Returns
chapters.summary: Elias comes back under pretext of follow-up, actually to warn Coral: her file has been flagged, a search is coming within days. He offers to falsify the census record. Beat: alliance forged across the desk.

chapters.title: The Great Storm
chapters.summary: The worst storm in living memory strikes early, trapping everyone. The light must be kept burning or boats—including Dara's with Greta aboard—will founder. Climax begins. Beat: nature stripping away all pretense.

chapters.title: Keeping the Light
chapters.summary: Coral and Elias work the mechanism together through the night, hands blistered, while Greta holds the lamp glass steady. The storm tries to take everything; they refuse. Beat: unity in extremis, the book's emotional peak.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Dawn: two boats lost, Dara's survived because the light held. But the search party arrives with the relief crew, and Greta is found. Coral steps forward and claims her openly as kin. Beat: invisibility voluntarily surrendered.

chapters.title: The Tribunal
chapters.summary: Coral testifies, producing Tomás's typed memoir and Heinrich's letters as evidence of loyalty, not treason. Elias corroborates at cost to his career. The room weighs her words. Beat: truth as defense, family as testimony.

chapters.title: Verdict
chapters.summary: Greta is granted leave to remain as a ward of the keeper; Coral is retained—not transferred—to train the automation crew. Elias chooses to stay on the island as its new recorder. Beat: justice imperfect but human.

chapters.title: What Cannot Be Carried
chapters.summary: Coral finally empties the trunk, giving away what she hoarded against departure, keeping only the typewriter and three cups. The islanders help rebuild the storm-damaged cottages. Beat: release, roots replacing readiness.

chapters.title: A Bridge for the Typewriter
chapters.summary: Epilogue, spring. Greta types letters to her father under Coral's dictation; the light burns automatic above them. Coral measures the world now not in what can be carried, but in who stayed. Final beat: home as a verb, not a place.
